messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a recap post about what a team learned at an industry conference. Around 250 words.

output:
Four of us went to KubeCon in Atlanta last week. Here is what stuck.

The hallway track beat the sessions, again. We came in with a list of talks and left with a list of names. A platform engineer from a mid-size logistics company spent forty minutes walking us through how they killed their internal PaaS after two years and moved everyone to raw Helm charts plus a good template repo. Their argument: the abstraction cost more to maintain than the thing it abstracted. We had been sketching a similar internal layer since June. That conversation saved us a quarter.

Two talks were worth the trip. Natasha Ridley's session on eBPF-based network policy showed real numbers from a 4,000-node cluster, including where the approach falls apart under high pod churn. And a lightning talk on OpenTelemetry collector configs convinced Marcus that our current sampling strategy is throwing away the traces we most need.

The vendor floor was thinner than last year and more honest about it. Fewer AI banners than we expected. Several booths we visited had shipped nothing since 2024 and said so when asked directly.

What we are changing: we are reviewing the internal platform proposal against the logistics team's postmortem before we write more code, and Marcus is auditing our tail sampling rules this sprint.

What we are not changing: nothing at the conference moved us on the service mesh question. We heard three incompatible recommendations and no data that separated them. That decision stays where it was.

Slides and our notes are in the shared drive under conferences/2026-kubecon.
